Terminology Without Consensus: A Thematic Analysis of Nomenclature Choice and Program Structure Among Expanded EMS Programs in a Single State.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Expanded emergency medical services (E-EMS) programs, such as mobile integrated health care (MIH) and community paramedicine (CP), are increasingly common in the United States (U.S.). Although an international consensus definition exists specifically for CP, the terminology used by active U.S. E-EMS programs is poorly described, yet has important implications for program visibility, stakeholder engagement, evaluation, and policy. We sought to characterize how E-EMS programs in a single state describe themselves and factors associated with their chosen terminology.
METHODS: We conducted a qualitative thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with E-EMS programs in Ohio. We used "E-EMS" as a historically established, neutral umbrella term to avoid prespecifying MIH, CP, or MIH-CP terminology during program identification. We identified E-EMS programs through voluntary reports to Ohio EMS, the Emergency Triage, Treat, and Transport (ET3) roster, publicly reported E-EMS programs on national dashboards, and snowball sampling. An interviewee from each E-EMS program participated in a recorded semi-structured interview focused on E-EMS program terminology, goals, services, and partnerships. Interview transcripts were reviewed by two coders, with discrepancies discussed with and adjudicated by a third reviewer. We used an inductive approach to develop the codebook, followed by thematic analysis to identify themes and subthemes.
RESULTS: We identified 58 E-EMS programs meeting inclusion criteria; 23 participated and were included in the analysis. Participants described inconsistent use and varying interpretation of common terms such as MIH, CP, or MIH-CP; one in four used alternative terminology (e.g., neighborhood paramedic, EMS outreach). Participants attributed their terminology choices to the variability in MIH definitions and to limited understanding of MIH or CP among patients or external stakeholders. Despite variation in program terminology, program goals were consistently focused on filling unmet community needs, and program services were uniformly described as adaptable and reliant upon partnerships outside of EMS.
CONCLUSIONS: The terminology used to describe E-EMS programs in a single state varied considerably. Despite this, E-EMS program goals and services were consistent, suggesting early convergence upon the core mission of E-EMS programs. Participants perceived inconsistent or unfamiliar terminology as a barrier to patient awareness, referral generation, and stakeholder engagement.

title: More Than a Tobacco Problem: Cigarette Smoking as a Marker of Poorer Cardiovascular Health Among Emergency Medical Services Clinicians.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Emergency medical services (EMS) work demands physical capacity, sustained alertness, and performance under stress, making cardiovascular health a workforce concern, not only a personal one. Cigarette smoking persists in portions of the EMS workforce, but whether it signals cardiovascular risk beyond tobacco exposure itself is unknown. We examined whether cigarette smoking was associated with poorer cardiovascular health across the non-tobacco domains of the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 (LE8) framework among nationally certified EMS clinicians.
METHODS: We conducted an observational study and cross-sectional secondary analysis of a voluntary survey offered to nationally certified emergency medical technicians (EMTs), advanced EMTs, and paramedics upon completion of recertification (October 2023-April 2024). To isolate associations beyond tobacco exposure, the primary outcome was a modified composite score (mLE7) averaging the seven non-nicotine LE8 domains (0-100 scale). Ideal cardiovascular health was defined as mLE7 ≥ 80. Multivariable linear and logistic regression models adjusted for demographic, educational, occupational, and organizational characteristics.
RESULTS: Among 36,436 survey respondents, 7,703 had complete data for smoking status and all seven non-nicotine domains. Of these, 48.8% had never smoked, 45.2% formerly smoked, and 6.0% currently smoked. Mean mLE7 scores were 59.2 among never smokers, 56.9 among former smokers, and 51.5 among current smokers. Compared with never smokers, current smokers had lower adjusted mLE7 scores (β, -6.02; 95% CI, -7.63 to -4.41) and lower odds of ideal cardiovascular health (aOR, 0.37; 95% CI, 0.23 to 0.61). Former smokers had intermediate results (β, -1.62; 95% CI, -2.37 to -0.87; aOR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.62 to 0.86). Current smoking was associated with poorer scores across diet, physical activity, sleep, blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood glucose domains (p < 0.05). Clinicians at private and hospital-based agencies had lower adjusted mLE7 scores than those at fire-based agencies.
CONCLUSIONS: Among EMS clinicians, current cigarette smoking was associated with poorer cardiovascular health across nearly every non-tobacco domain, suggesting that smoking may serve as a readily identifiable marker of broader cardiovascular risk in this workforce. Agencies may consider pairing cessation support with broader cardiovascular health initiatives for clinicians who smoke. Sensitivity analyses addressing missing data yielded consistent results.

title: Frequency of On-Scene Goal-Directed Field Interventions for Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in a Regional System of Care.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Early on-scene resuscitation improves outcomes from pediatric non-traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA); however, for pediatric patients, the early evacuation strategy remains commonplace. We sought to determine the frequency of goal-directed interventions initiated by paramedics prior to transport for pediatric patients with OHCA in a regional emergency medical services (EMS) system.
METHODS: In this retrospective observational study and cross-sectional analysis, we analyzed the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (CARES) and linked electronic patient care reports (ePCR) data for patients aged <15 years treated by EMS for nontraumatic OHCA in Los Angeles (LA) County from January 2021 to December 2022. The primary outcome was the frequency of goal-directed therapies administered on scene prior to transport, which we defined as defibrillation for shockable rhythms and administration of epinephrine and fluid resuscitation for non-shockable rhythms. We also tabulated descriptive statistics regarding arrest characteristics, scene times, frequency of other prehospital treatments, and patient outcomes.
RESULTS: Among 176 eligible pediatric OHCA cases analyzed in CARES, 112 (64%) were male, the median age was 10 months (IQR 3-51), and 162 (92%) had an initial non-shockable rhythm. Of these, 156 patients were successfully linked to electronic patient care report (ePCR) records for analyses of prehospital interventions. Among 143 patients with non-shockable rhythms, EMS administered epinephrine before transport in 58 (41%) and fluids in 12 (8%). Among 13 patients with shockable rhythms, EMS delivered defibrillation before transport in 11 (85%). Bag-valve-mask (BVM) use was documented in 80 (51%) patients, although its timing relative to scene departure could not be determined. Median on-scene time was 10 minutes (IQR 5-18). Ten patients (6%) survived to hospital discharge, including 6 (3%) with a favorable neurologic outcome.
CONCLUSIONS: In this regional EMS system, fewer than half of patients with non-shockable rhythms received a dose of epinephrine and fewer than one in ten received intravenous fluids prior to transport, whereas most patients with shockable rhythms were defibrillated on scene. Further work is needed to identify barriers to timely delivery of on-scene resuscitative interventions.

title: Total gastric and intragastric air volumes in immediate post-resuscitation whole-body computed tomography after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: Association with airway management, aspiration, diaphragmatic position and initial blood gas analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Gastric distension (GD) may occur during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), but quantitative human data after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remain limited. We quantified gastric volumes after OHCA and explored associations with prehospital airway strategy, CT-defined aspiration, diaphragmatic position, and initial blood gases.
METHODS: This retrospective single-center study included OHCA patients undergoing post-resuscitation whole-body computed tomography (CT) within 180 minutes of emergency department (ED) admission between January 1, 2020, and March 31, 2025. Total gastric volume (TGV) and intragastric air volume (GAV) were quantified by CT volumetry.
RESULTS: Of 255 identified patients, 120 underwent CT within 180 minutes. Median TGV was 594 mL and correlated strongly with GAV (p < 0.001). Among patients with an advanced airway at ED arrival, neither TGV (p = 0.20) nor GAV (p = 0.24) differed significantly between the tracheal airway (TA; n = 87) and supraglottic airway (SGA; n = 28) groups. CT-defined aspiration was numerically more frequent with SGA than TA (78.6% vs. 57.5%; OR 2.7; p = 0.071), whereas neither TGV nor GAV was associated with CT-defined aspiration. Weak positive correlations were observed between initial pCO2 and both TGV (ρ = 0.16; one-tailed p = 0.037) and GAV (ρ = 0.19; one-tailed p = 0.018).
CONCLUSION: Gastric volumes were high in this selected post-OHCA immediate CT (< 180 minutes) cohort. No significant differences were detected according to recorded prehospital airway strategy, and gastric volume was not associated with CT-defined aspiration. Mechanisms and clinical consequences remain uncertain and require prospective studies before preventive/ therapeutic implications can be established.

title: What's Blood Got to Do with It? Identifying MPDS® Dispatch Codes Most Commonly Associated with Prehospital Blood Administration.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to identify Medical Priority Dispatch System (MPDS®) codes most frequently associated with prehospital blood utilization.
METHODS: We examined Delaware's prehospital blood database to determine dispatch codes where low titer group O positive whole blood (LTOWB) was administered. We calculated the number of blood units under each dispatch code within the study period (May 2023- February 2026). Using this data, we identified the MPDS® codes associated with the highest number of blood units, including the top five codes overall, top medical codes, and as well as blood utilization rates for penetrating versus blunt traumas.
RESULTS: The most frequent blood utilization came from the following dispatch codes: 29D02 (traffic collision, high mechanism) 32 patients, 27D04G (penetrating trauma with central wounds) 32 patients, 29D02M (auto versus pedestrian) 28 patients, 29D05 (traffic collision with entrapment) 24 patients, and 29D02L (auto versus bicycle/motorcycle) 20 patients. These five dispatch codes accounted for 29% of all prehospital LTOWB utilized within the 33-month study period. Analyzing blood utilization for non-traumatic dispatch codes revealed: 21D04/21D04M (dangerous hemorrhage, medical) 18 patients, 21D03/21D03M (hemorrhage, not alert, medical) 13 patients, 9E01/M9E01/M9E02 (cardiac or respiratory arrest/death, not breathing) 13 patients, and 21D05/21D05M (hemorrhage, abnormal breathing, medical) 7 patients. These four dispatch codes accounted for 11% (51 patients) of LTOWB utilization. When performing odds ratio analysis to determine odds of blood administration, we found 27D04G, 29D02M, and 29D02L to be statistically significant with 95% confidence intervals of [0.35- 0.87], [2.42- 5.72], [1.47- 3.91], and odds ratios of 0.55, 3.72, and 2.40, respectively. Additionally, our analysis demonstrated that patients with MPDS® coding for penetrating trauma with a delta level priority (27D) have higher likelihood of prehospital blood administration than delta priority high mechanism traffic incidents (29D). This comparison showed an OR of 10.40 that blood would be given to the penetrating trauma patient with a 95% confidence interval of [7.93- 13.66].
CONCLUSIONS: Specific MPDS® codes are strongly associated with prehospital blood utilization. Identifying these patterns offers a unique opportunity for emergency medical services systems to implement automatic blood dispatch protocols based on dispatch code.

title: Prolonged Onboard Storage of Red Blood Cells in Ground Ambulances for Prehospital Transfusion: A Real-World Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Permanent onboard storage of red blood cells (RBC) units could facilitate timely prehospital transfusion but may expose blood products to cumulative transport-related mechanical stress. We evaluated the quality of RBC units stored continuously in operational ground ambulances under real-world emergency medical service conditions.
METHODS: In this randomized controlled experimental study of RBC units, leukoreduced RBC units were randomly assigned to continuous onboard ambulance storage from day 7 to day 42 (n = 12) or standard blood bank storage at 2-6 °C for 42 days (n = 14). Samples were analyzed on days 7, 28, and 42. The primary outcome was hemolysis. Secondary outcomes included plasma biochemistry and storage-induced microerythrocytes (SMEs), an emerging morphological marker associated with post-transfusion RBC recovery. Temporal trajectories of SME levels were assessed using repeated-measures multivariate analysis of variance and fixed-effects panel models.
RESULTS: All RBC units remained below the European regulatory hemolysis threshold of 0.8% at day 42. Hemolysis was higher in ambulance-stored units at day 28 (Hodges-Lehmann difference, +0.043 percentage points; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.010-0.076; p = 0.015) and day 42 (+0.096 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.029-0.176; p = 0.008). The SME levels increased in both groups, with a significant time-by-group interaction (p = 0.034) indicating different temporal trajectories. Additional SME accumulation in ambulance-stored units occurred predominantly between days 28 and 42. At day 42, the mean between-group SME difference was +9.04 percentage points (95% CI, -0.66 to 18.73; p = 0.066). The available sample was insufficient to exclude moderate or larger between-group differences. Biochemical changes were broadly similar between groups.
CONCLUSIONS: Continuous onboard RBC storage in operational ground ambulances maintained all units within regulatory hemolysis limits through day 42. However, higher hemolysis and late divergence in SME accumulation suggest that prolonged ambulance exposure may influence RBC storage quality. These findings provide preliminary support for the feasibility of continuous onboard RBC storage, particularly earlier in the storage period, but do not establish equivalence with conventional blood bank storage.

title: Prehospital Trauma Compendium: Prehospital Management of Pediatric Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Circulatory Arrest - A Joint Position Statement and Resource Document of NAEMSP, ACS-COT, ACEP, and AAP.
abstract: In 2014 the National Association of EMS Physicians (NAEMSP), American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma (ACS-COT), American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP), and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) published the first joint position statement discussing withholding and discontinuing resuscitation attempts for pediatric traumatic out-of-hospital circulatory arrest (TOHCA). Since then, the body of literature addressing pediatric TOHCA has evolved and evidence has grown that demonstrates the nearly uniformly poor prognosis of children who suffer circulatory arrest in the prehospital setting as a result of trauma. To support emergency medical services (EMS) clinicians in their approach to these high-acuity, low-frequency, and challenging cases, this project aimed to update guidance regarding decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts for pediatric traumatic circulatory arrest. NAEMSP, ACEP, ACS-COT, and AAP recommend:EMS resuscitation of pediatric TOHCA should:Prioritize prompt identification of patients who may benefit from transport to definitive care at trauma centers when safe and appropriate. On-scene resuscitation should be balanced against the potential benefit of transfer to a proximate trauma center.Emphasize the identification of reversible causes of traumatic circulatory arrest and timely use of clinically indicated life-saving interventions (LSIs) within the EMS clinician's scope of practice. These include:External hemorrhage control with direct pressure, wound packing, and tourniquetsAirway management using the least-invasive airway interventions required to achieve and maintain airway patency, oxygenation, and adequate ventilation.Chest decompression if clinical concern for tension pneumothorax. Empiric bilateral decompression is not recommended in the absence of suspected thoracic trauma.External chest compressions and ventilations have a larger role in pediatric TOHCA resuscitation than in adult TOHCA resuscitation, with children frequently having TOHCA secondary to head injury, hypoxia and other non-hemorrhagic mechanisms. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should be provided when the cause of circulatory arrest is unclear.Epinephrine is of lower priority than other LSIs.Consider point of care ultrasound (POCUS) to guide decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts.Resuscitation attempts may be withheld in pediatric TOHCA patients with:Injuries that are incompatible with life (e.g., decapitation, hemi-corpectomy, incineration).Evidence of prolonged circulatory arrest (e.g., rigor mortis, dependent lividity, decomposition).Advanced care planning documents that indicate Do Not Resuscitate (DNR)/ Do Not Attempt Resuscitation (DNAR)/Allow Natural Death medical orders.Resuscitation attempts may be discontinued in pediatric TOHCA patients who:Have no return of spontaneous circulation after provision of at least 15 minutes of high-quality CPR in addition to performance of other lifesaving interventions directed at treating potentially reversible causes of pediatric TOHCA. Longer durations of CPR, up to 30 minutes, may be considered for patients with positive predictors of survival such as organized rhythm, witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, or with proximate access to a trauma center.Have known predictors of very low probability of survival such as penetrating trauma without proximate access to a trauma center, asystole, unwitnessed arrest, or lack of bystander CPR.Protocols guiding decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation of pediatric TOHCA benefit from oversight by EMS physicians in collaboration with pediatric experts and local or regional trauma system stakeholders. Implementation of such protocols for pediatric patients benefits from involvement of community stakeholders including family representatives, law enforcement, medical examiner, and child fatality review committees.Considerations for protocol implementation include local resource availability, EMS clinician and public safety, psychosocial support to surviving family members and emergency responders, and dignified handling of the deceased patient.Training needs for EMS clinicians include techniques to communicate with family members regarding the death of a child and understanding the clinician's own response to this low-frequency, high-emotion experience.

Survival after neonatal chest compressions at birth: Temporal trends and prognostic factors in a population-based cohort, Queensland, Australia.
abstract:
AIM: To examine temporal trends and prognostic factors for 28-day survival among infants receiving chest compressions (CC) in Queensland, Australia.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective population-based cohort study using the Queensland Perinatal Data Collection (2008-2024), including all liveborn CC recipients at birth. Temporal trends in crude 28-day survival were examined overall and by gestational age (GA) groups. Multivariable generalised estimating equations were used to identify factors independently associated with survival while accounting for clustering within birthing locations.
RESULTS: Among 3,077 CC recipients, 70.5% established regular spontaneous breathing within 60 minutes of birth, and 89.0% survived to 28 days. Crude 28-day survival improved from 82% in 2008 to 89% in 2024 and was consistently higher in term (GA ≥37+0 weeks) than preterm infants. Compared with term infants, adjusted odds of survival declined with decreasing GA: 32+0 to 36+6 weeks (aOR 0.56, 95% CI 0.40-0.77), 28+0 to 31+6 weeks (aOR 0.35, 95% CI 0.23-0.54), and <28+0 weeks (aOR 0.17, 95% CI 0.12-0.23). However, after adjusting for cord pH or epinephrine administration, survival in infants born at 32+0 to 36+6 weeks did not differ significantly from term infants.
CONCLUSION: Survival to 28 days among CC recipients was high and increased over time. Lower gestational age was the strongest independent prognostic factor for mortality, although the survival difference between term and moderate-to-late preterm infants was attenuated after adjustment for cord pH or epinephrine administration. Prospective studies assessing CC indications and measures of resuscitation quality are needed to optimise neonatal resuscitation and improve outcomes.

title: Survival after out of hospital cardiac arrest in relation to AED usage in a multi response system including AED equipped drones.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early defibrillation is a key determinant of survival in out‑of‑hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). In multi-response systems, it remains unclear which responders contribute most to early AED use and survival. This study compared first AED-attaching responders and their association with 30-day survival in a regional multi-response system.
METHODS: This registry‑based cohort study included OHCA cases in Västra Götaland Region, Sweden, between January 1, 2015, and December 31, 2024. Data were obtained from EMS, dispatch, and registry databases. The primary outcome was 30‑day survival.
RESULTS: Among 9,413 OHCAs, EMS attached the first AED in 72% of cases, followed by on-duty first responders (ODFR) (18%), bystanders (6.0%), and community first responders (CFR) (4.5%). EMS attachment decreased from 77% to 67%, whereas CFR involvement increased from 1% to 13%. 30‑day survival was highest when AEDs were attached by bystanders (28%), compared with 9.0% for EMS, 8.7% for ODFR and 8.6% for CFR. Among witnessed OHCAs with an initial shockable rhythm, 30-day survival was highest in bystander-attached cases (62%), compared with 36% for CFR, 32% for ODFR, and 24% for EMS. In the multivariable analysis, bystander AED attachment was associated with higher odds of 30‑day survival compared with EMS (OR 2.25; 95% CI 1.77-2.85).
CONCLUSION: In this multi-response system, survival was highest when AEDs were first attached by bystanders and remained higher after adjustment for known prognostic factors. This association likely reflects earlier access to defibrillation. These findings suggest that improving immediate access to defibrillation may have the greatest impact on OHCA outcomes.

title: Early Prehospital Prediction of Neurological Outcome After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Derivation and External Validation of the MIRA-29 Score.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Out-of-hospital cardiac (OHCA) arrest is a frequent emergency, and few patients will survive with good neurological outcome. Identification of patients with a low likelihood of meaningful recovery represents a major clinical challenge. Numerous scores have been developed to guide decision-making after OHCA, with variable goals and targets, but most of them have been validated on small cohorts, integrates variables not available in the prehospital field, or do have low prediction values. MIRA-29 score aimed to only rely on simple clinical variables, available in the prehospital setting. We hypothetized that such score will provide incremental neurological prognosis value at an early-stage following OHCA.
METHODS: MIRA-29 score was derived and internally validated over a five-year period on a prospective cohort of 1099 adult patients, including all OHCA treated by our territory dispatch center. Multivariate analysis identified independent variables within the database, that were used to optimize the prediction model using machine-learning and genetic algorithms. The score was subsequently validated externally on 82 696 patients extracted from the French national cardiac arrest registry (RéAC).
RESULTS: Out from the 1099 patients, 85 patients (7.7%) had a favorable neurological outcome. Multivariate analysis identified five independent variables associated with neurological outcome: age, low-flow duration, number of external electric shock, epinephrine dose, and the OHCA site (street, public facility, home). After model optimization and machine-learning, age was not retained within the final model. External validation depicted a precision of 0.86 and a recall of 0.88 of the model. The F1-Score and accuracy are respectively 0.87 and 0.88, and specificity for a bad neurological prognosis is 0.99.
CONCLUSION: MIRA‑29 strength lies on its ability to reliably identify patients with extremely high probability of poor neurological outcome, while being based on four simple clinical variables. The prospective validation of MIRA-29 in the clinical setting may evaluate its impact on clinical decision making.

title: RescQTM: One-year implementation and feasibility results of a digitally enabled support pathway for bystanders of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Bystanders to out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) are at significant risk of psychological distress, yet no standardised support pathway exists for them in the UK. RescQ™ is a digital-first bystander support pathway embedded within regional prehospital and cardiac arrest care services.
AIM: To evaluate the feasibility of embedding RescQ™ into routine emergency medical services (EMS) practice leading to appropriate contact with bystanders involved in OHCA. Secondary aims were to describe digital access, demand for liaison officer (LO) support, identification of younger bystanders, and EMS clinician acceptability.
METHODS: Prospective one-year regional service evaluation of RescQ™ across Essex, UK. Bystanders involved in eligible OHCA events were registered by EMS clinicians and provided with immediate access to secure digital resources. Bystanders could self-refer for additional support through LO.
RESULTS: During the one-year evaluation, 220 of 432 eligible OHCA incidents had at least one bystander identified and the incident entered into the RescQ™ pathway, representing an incident-level capture rate of 50.9%. Across these incidents, 298 bystanders were identified, of whom 260 eligible adults were registered with RescQ™. Of registered adult bystanders, 96.2% accessed the digital resources at least once. Among all identified bystanders, 30/298 (10.1%) were aged under 18 years. Approximately 10% of registered bystanders self-referred for additional personalised LO support. Among 25 EMS clinician survey respondents who had used RescQTM in clinical practice, ratings indicated acceptability.
CONCLUSION: RescQ™ demonstrated the feasibility of identifying and supporting bystanders following OHCA through a digitally enabled pathway, achieving incident-level capture above the pre-specified feasibility threshold and high website access among registered adults. These findings support further multi-region evaluation of implementation, sustainability and scalability across different EMS systems.

title: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrests due to foreign body airway obstruction: A CanROC registry, retrospective cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Foreign body airway obstruction (FBAO) is a treatable cause of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but North American data are limited.
METHODS: Exploratory retrospective cohort study of EMS-treated OHCAs using the Canadian Resuscitation Outcomes Consortium (CanROC) registry (2005-2023), classified as obviously FBAO-related or of no obvious cause (presumed cardiac). Logistic regression compared Utstein characteristics between etiologies and identified factors associated with prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and survival to acute care discharge.
RESULTS: Among 105,178 EMS-treated OHCAs, 1,106(1.1%) were obviously FBAO-related. Compared with cases of no obvious cause, obviously FBAO-related cases were older (median 73 vs 68 years, p<0.001), more often witnessed (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 6.98[5.36-9.25]), more often attended by trained bystanders (aOR 3.30[2.41-4.41]), and less often had a shockable rhythm (aOR 0.11[0.07-0.15]). Obviously FBAO-related cases more often achieved prehospital ROSC (62.7% vs 37.8%; OR 2.77[2.44-3.13]), but survival did not differ (10.6% vs 9.0%,p=0.094). Within the obviously FBAO-related cohort, ROSC was associated with witnessed arrest (aOR 1.66[1.13-2.43]) and shorter EMS response time (aOR 0.95 per minute[0.92-0.99]). Survival was associated with younger age (aOR 0.76 per decade[0.61-0.93]), initial shockable rhythm (aOR 4.76[1.55-13.30]), and shorter EMS response time (aOR 0.81 per minute[0.66-0.98]). Survival was 18.1% and 0.8% among obviously FBAO-related OHCAs with and without prehospital ROSC, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS: Obviously FBAO-related OHCAs are uncommon but clinically distinct. ROSC is frequent, yet survival remains low and is associated with early prehospital factors, supporting choking prevention initiatives, bystander training, and rapid EMS response.

title: Commercially available multimodal LLMs for EEG-based prognostication after cardiac arrest.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Machine-learning and deep-learning approaches have been successfully applied to EEG-based prognostication in comatose patients after cardiac arrest (CA), but typically rely on task-specific signal processing, feature extraction, and model development. Here, we investigated whether two commercially available multimodal large language models (LLMs) could predict neurological outcome directly from EEG images.
METHODS: Thirty-three comatose patients on the first day after CA from a prospective cohort were included. For each patient, a single 10-second EEG segment displayed using a longitudinal bipolar montage was rendered as PNG image. ChatGPT 5.4. and Claude Opus 4.7 were instructed to estimate the probability for favorable outcome for each case based on the EEG and a generic information block describing conditions of recordings. Five different prompting strategies were used, including few-shot prompting where four exemplary EEGs (not from the 33 patients) were provided. Predictive performance was quantified using AUC and accuracy.
RESULTS: Across prompting strategies, the AUC ranged from 0.86 to 0.99 for ChatGPT and from 0.74 to 1.00 for Claude. The highest accuracy achieved by both models was 93.9% using few-shot prompting. As reference, a previously published dedicated deep-learning model achieved 100% on the same cohort.
CONCLUSION: In this exploratory study of a small cohort, multimodal LLMs showed variable but potentially promising discrimination for predicting favorable outcome from single EEG image in comatose patients after CA. Performance depended substantially on prompt design. These findings require confirmation in a larger cohort.

title: Community First Responder Activation Reduces the Negative Impact of AED Distance on Bystander Defibrillation After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Early defibrillation is critical for survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), yet bystander defibrillation remains uncommon despite the availability of automated external defibrillators (AEDs). We investigated whether HeartRunner community first responder activation increased the likelihood of bystander defibrillation and 30-day survival in relation to the distance to the nearest accessible AED.
METHODS: Linking data from the Danish Cardiac Arrest Registry, Danish AED Network, and HeartRunner application, we identified patients with OHCA eligible for HeartRunner activation during 2017-2021. Using street-network distances to the nearest accessible AED, we examined associations between HeartRunner activation, bystander defibrillation, and 30-day survival using multivariable logistic regression with interaction terms and targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE).
RESULTS: Among 5,753 OHCAs (median age, 74 years; 64% male; 78% in private locations), HeartRunner activation (41%) was associated with higher bystander defibrillation across AED distances (p-interaction = 0.004), with no interaction for 30-day survival (p-interaction = 0.054). Predicted bystander defibrillation with versus without HeartRunner activation was 9.6% vs 5.5% at Q1 (389 m), 10.0% vs 4.3% at median (717 m), and 13.0% vs 4.8% at Q3 (1,183 m). TMLE estimated a 6.1-percentage-point higher probability of bystander defibrillation (95% CI, 4.5-7.8; p<0.001) and a modest 1.8-percentage-point increase in 30-day survival (95% CI, 0.1-3.6; p=0.038) with HeartRunner activation.
CONCLUSION: HeartRunner activation attenuated the decline in bystander defibrillation with increasing AED distance following OHCA, without a corresponding distance interaction for 30-day survival. Overall, TMLE supported higher bystander defibrillation and suggested a modest increase in 30-day survival with HeartRunner activation.

title: A Mobile Application Improves Paramedic Performance in Simulated Trauma Care: A Crossover Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Clinical performance during prehospital trauma care varies among emergency medical services (EMS) clinicians, particularly during high-stress critical responses. We developed a mobile application providing real-time access to local treatment protocols, decision support tools, and instructional procedure videos to supplement standard practice. We evaluated whether use of the application improved paramedic performance during simulated trauma scenarios.
METHODS: We conducted a crossover randomized controlled trial between July 2025 and February 2026 comparing standard care alone with standard care plus the mobile application during two high-fidelity trauma simulations (one adult and one pediatric). Paramedics, working in pairs, were block randomized to one of four sequences, varying both the scenario order and the application use. Performance was assessed using predefined critical actions; completing all critical actions was required to successfully complete the scenario. A generalized linear mixed model with a binomial distribution and logit link function was used for each paramedic pair to estimate the adjusted odds ratio (OR) for successfully completing a scenario with or without the application.
RESULTS: Of 112 paramedics, 98 (88%) participated, forming 49 pairs. One pair withdrew before study completion, leaving 48 pairs for analysis. For scenarios using the application, 17/48 (35.4%) successfully completed the scenario compared to 3/48 (6.3%) for scenarios not using the application, adjusted odds 8.28 (95% CI 2.21-31.09). Among scenarios using the application, 10/25 (40%) adult scenarios and 7/23 (30.4%) pediatric scenarios met successful completion criteria compared to 3/23 (13%) adult and 0/25 (0%) pediatric with standard practice alone. User experience survey results demonstrated that participating paramedics assessed the application as being practical to use and valuable for clinical care.
CONCLUSIONS: Use of the mobile decision support application improves odds of performing high-quality clinical care in simulated trauma patient scenarios. Further studies are needed to evaluate performance and usability in a field environment.

title: Five-Year Experience with Automated Head Up Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Automated head-up position cardiopulmonary resuscitation (AHUP-CPR), the combination of a head and thorax positioning device, active compression-decompression CPR, and an impedance threshold device, lowers intracranial pressure and increases cerebral blood flow and neurologically favorable survival in animal models versus conventional CPR (C-CPR).
METHODS: This prospective, observational, investigator-initiated registry study reports 5-year multi-center outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) from areas served by emergency medical services (EMS) agencies that implemented AHUP-CPR as their routine first-responder standard of care. Adults with non-traumatic OHCA were initially treated with immediate conventional (C-CPR) followed by rapid transition to AHUP-CPR. The primary study focus was on patients who survived to hospital discharge with favorable neurological function (HD-FN). Additional analyses included assessment of sustained return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to hospital discharge (HD), outcomes based upon the presenting rhythm, and impact of covariates on HD-FN.
RESULTS: Ten EMS agencies serving 1.5 million people across nine U.S. states contributed data to the AHUP-CPR Registry. A total of 3,709 OHCA patients met enrollment criteria. Across five years, (2020-2024), the average (± SD) interval from 9-1-1 call receipt-to-professional CPR was 9.62 ± 5.78 min. Incidence of ROSC, HD, and HD-FN were 29.5%, 13.1%, and 10.5%, respectively. The incidence of HD-FN for patients presenting with a shockable rhythm meeting Utstein criteria, pulseless electrical activity, or asystole were 33.9%, 11.8%, and 2.0%, respectively. Among 391 neurologically favorable survivors, 91% had a Cerebral Performance Category score of 1 (normal or near normal brain function) at HD. The average age of the survivors was 56.8 ± 16.3 years. Age, interval from 9-1-1 call to professional CPR, witnessed status, and initial rhythm were the most significant predictors of HD-FN using multivariable Poisson regression.
CONCLUSIONS: In this 5-year observational registry study, use of AHUP-CPR for the treatment of OHCA was associated with survival to HD of 13.1% and HD-FN of 10.5% in the overall cohort, which comprised patients presenting in shockable rhythms, PEA, and asystole. Drawn from 3,709 OHCA patients treated across diverse EMS systems, these findings provide the largest clinical practice-based characterization to date of the outcomes associated with early transition to AHUP-CPR.

title: Prehospital Resource Utilization After Video-Assisted Versus Telephone-Only Emergency Calls: A Post Hoc Analysis of the CAM-VISION Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To examine whether video assistance during emergency calls reduced actual prehospital resource utilization across the complete response pathway compared with telephone-only calls.
METHODS: This post hoc analysis included 18,745 calls from the cluster-randomized CAM-VISION parent trial (NCT05742412; 8,124 video; 10,621 telephone only). Outcomes were assessed at call level according to telecommunicator allocation and included unit dispatch, pathway progression, number of units, and cumulative unit time. Effects were estimated with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) accounting for clustering by telecommunicator.
RESULTS: Initial unit dispatch occurred in 69.4% of video-group calls and 73.9% of telephone-only calls (risk difference, -4.5 percentage points; 95% confidence intervals (CI) (-10.0 to 1.0). Among calls with no unit initially dispatched, subsequent unit dispatch was uncommon (5.1% vs 5.5%). Across the complete response pathway, 71.0% versus 75.3% received at least 1 unit (risk difference, -4.4 percentage points; 95% CI, -9.6 to 0.8), and 69.3% versus 73.8% had a unit reach the scene (risk difference, -4.5 percentage points; 95% CI, -10.0 to 1.0). More than 1 unit was dispatched in 23.3% versus 25.0%. Mean units per call were 1.005 versus 1.054 (mean difference, -0.049; 95% CI, -0.148 to 0.049); mean cumulative unit time was 52.8 versus 54.3 minutes (mean difference, -1.5; 95% CI, -6.2 to 3.1). Overall, differences in initial dispatch were concentrated in ambulance use.
CONCLUSIONS: No statistically significant absolute differences in conventional prehospital resource utilization were observed. Point estimates were consistently lower in the video group, primarily through fewer initial dispatches, and subsequent dispatch did not materially offset this numerical difference.

title: Does critical care training explain higher survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest?, Letter to the Editor.
Trends in United States Pediatric In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Incidence and Mortality in a Nationally Representative Sample, 2009-2022.
abstract:
AIM: National estimates of pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) incidence in the United States rely on a voluntary registry that may underrepresent smaller and critical access hospitals. Administrative datasets offer a nationally representative alternative. We estimated nationally representative pediatric IHCA incidence and mortality trends from 2009 through 2022.
METHODS: Serial cross-sectional analysis of five triennial editions of the Kids' Inpatient Database (2009-2022), identifying IHCA in children <18 years by ICD-9 (99.60, 99.63) and ICD-10 (5A12012) cardiopulmonary resuscitation procedure codes. Two hospitals with implausible CPR rates were excluded. Survey-weighted incidence per 1,000 hospitalizations and in-hospital mortality among resuscitated children were estimated overall and by neonatal status, complex chronic condition (CCC) status, ZIP-code income quartile, and US Census region. Trends were tested with survey-weighted quasi-Poisson regression across the full period and, as exploratory analyses, within the ICD-10 era (2016-2022).
RESULTS: Observed IHCA incidence was 1.11/1,000 in 2009 and 1.22/1,000 in 2012, decreased to 1.11/1,000 at the ICD-10 transition and increased to 1.35/1,000 by 2022. IHCA incidence in children hospitalized with a CCC rose from 3.26 to 6.60/1,000 (6.2%/year, p<0.001), while incidence without CCC remained low. Incidence varied by socioeconomic status (lowest vs highest income quartile 1.78 vs 1.04/1,000 in 2022). In-hospital mortality ranged from 34.1% (2012) to 40.4% (2019), whereas IHCA deaths per 1,000 hospitalizations increased 1.7%/year (p<0.001), concentrated among children with a CCC.
CONCLUSION: The incidence of pediatric IHCA increased among hospitalizations involving children with CCC and was higher among children who live in lower income areas. In-hospital mortality after CPR was largely stable, whereas arrest-related deaths per 1,000 hospitalizations increased among children with CCC. A single hospital's coding practices can materially distort national administrative estimates. What is already known Pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest affects approximately 15,200 children annually in the United States, with this national estimate derived primarily from a voluntary registry that may underrepresent smaller and critical access hospitals. Administrative databases offer nationally representative coverage but rely on procedure codes that are susceptible to misclassification. What this study adds In this nationally representative administrative database sample spanning 2009-2022, this study demonstrated that: 1) the incidence of IHCA among children with complex chronic conditions (CCC) rose steadily and accounted for the substantial majority of events, 2) the overall IHCA incidence was higher among children who live in lower income areas with the gradient worsening over the period evaluated, and 3) in-hospital mortality after CPR increased only slightly (34-40%), whereas arrest-related deaths per 1,000 hospitalizations increased more, driven mainly by rising incidence among children with CCC, and 4) CPR coding at a single hospital can substantially distort national administrative estimates.

title: Reply to: Does critical care training explain higher survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest?
Cost-effectiveness of paramedic-administered prehospital thrombolysis for ST elevation myocardial infarction.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Guidelines recommend prehospital thrombolysis for ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) if trained clinicians can interpret 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) on site. The Queensland Ambulance Service (QAS) has a well-established prehospital reperfusion program under which all paramedics are trained in prehospital STEMI diagnosis on 12-lead ECG and administering thrombolysis in the field to eligible patients. Whilst the clinical benefits of this treatment are proven, its cost-effectiveness remains to be established.
METHODS: We developed a decision-analytic microsimulation model to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of paramedic-administered thrombolysis for prehospital STEMI in the state of Queensland, Australia. The comparator was a hypothetical counterfactual group of patients who were clinically eligible for prehospital thrombolysis but received an alternate treatment pathway. The analysis was conducted from a health provider (Queensland Government) perspective. A lifetime time horizon was used. Input values of the acute phase were derived from our prehospital and linked hospital database of all STEMI patients receiving prehospital thrombolysis from QAS paramedics between January 2022 and December 2024. Input values of the long-term phase were obtained from published literature. Cost was expressed in Australian dollars (AUD) and United States dollars (USD) in 2026 value, and effectiveness in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs).
RESULTS: Prehospital thrombolysis improved outcomes at a cost of AUD 16,750.22 per QALY gained (95% uncertainty range AUD 15,477.48 - 18,422.84) or USD 11,725.15 (USD 10,834.24 - 12,895.99). In the sensitivity analysis, the cost-effectiveness of prehospital thrombolysis was robust to changes in input values.
CONCLUSIONS: Paramedic-administered thrombolysis in the field for prehospital STEMI, compared with no such treatment, represents value for money.

title: A Lighter Approach to Language Access: Virtual Interpreter Utilization in Emergency Medical Services (EMS).
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Limited English Proficiency (LEP) may create communication barriers during prehospital care. Although on-demand interpreter services are often available to emergency medical services (EMS) clinicians, utilization may be limited by device accessibility, workflow barriers, and clinician adoption. Our objective was to evaluate whether implementation of agency-issued lightweight clinician-carried smartphones was associated with increased utilization of virtual interpreter services during prehospital care.
METHODS: We conducted an observational retrospective pre-post cohort study of virtual interpreter service utilization within a large multistate Midwest EMS agency. On June 1, 2025, the agency issued smartphones (Apple iPhone 16, ∼6 ounces) to all clinicians, providing continuous access to virtual audio and video interpreter services (LanguageLine Solutions). Previously, interpreter services were accessed using large Toughbook laptops (∼6.1 pounds). Interpreter utilization was compared between pre-implementation (October 30, 2024, to May 31, 2025) and post-implementation (June 1, 2025, to December 31, 2025) periods. Interpreter requests per 100 encounters were compared using rate ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
RESULTS: Interpreter requests increased from 104 pre-implementation (0.19 per 100 encounters, 95% CI: 0.15-0.23) to 326 post-implementation (0.57 per 100 encounters, 95% CI: 0.51-0.63; RR= 3.04, 95% CI: 2.44-3.79; p < 0.001). Audio requests increased from 68 calls (0.12 per 100 encounters) to 271 calls (0.47 per 100 encounters; RR = 3.86, 95% CI: 2.96-5.03; p < 0.001). Video requests increased from 36 calls (0.06 per 100 encounters) to 55 calls (0.10 per 100 encounters), although the observed increase did not reach statistical significance (RR= 1.48, 95% CI: 0.97-2.25; p = 0.066). The most commonly requested languages were Spanish (n = 153, 36%), Somali (n = 146, 34%), and Arabic (n = 41, 10%).
CONCLUSIONS: Implementation of agency-issued lightweight clinician-carried smartphones was associated with a threefold increase in virtual interpreter utilization. This increase was driven primarily by audio interpretation, while the observed increase in video utilization did not reach statistical significance. These findings suggest that improving point-of-care accessibility of interpreter services through lightweight mobile devices may facilitate greater utilization during prehospital encounters with patients with LEP.

title: Impact of the COVID-19 Pandemic on Ambulance Transport for Suspected Bacterial Pneumonia and In-Hospital Mortality: A Population-Based ORION Study.
abstract:
AIM: To evaluate changes in difficult ambulance transport, in-hospital mortality, and ambulance transport rates for suspected bacterial pneumonia before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic in Osaka, Japan.
METHODS: This retrospective study used the population-based Osaka Emergency Information Research Intelligent Operation Network (ORION) registry (2018-2023). Patients with pneumonia (ICD-10 codes J13-J18) were identified independently using emergency medical technician diagnoses for transport analyses and physician diagnoses for mortality analyses. Periods were pre-pandemic (2018-2019), pandemic (2020-2022), and recovery (2023). Difficult transport was defined as four or more hospital selections and at least 30 min on scene. Annual ambulance transport rates and population-based in-hospital mortality were calculated per 100,000 residents.
RESULTS: Among 78,720 patients with suspected pneumonia identified by emergency medical technicians, difficult transport increased from 2.7% before the pandemic to 10.3% during the pandemic and 9.3% in recovery. Among 65,510 patients with physician-diagnosed pneumonia, in-hospital mortality was 7.8%, 10.7%, and 9.1%, respectively. Difficult transport was associated with higher in-hospital mortality (adjusted odds ratio, 1.14; 95% confidence interval, 1.03-1.25). Population-based in-hospital mortality showed no corresponding increase. Annual ambulance transport rates decreased from 166.3 per 100,000 residents in 2018 to 117.3 in 2021, returning to 167.0 in 2023.
CONCLUSIONS: During the pandemic, difficult transport and in-hospital mortality increased while ambulance transport rates for suspected pneumonia decreased. Changes in patient selection and case mix may partly explain the mortality trend.

title: Long-term outcomes and quality of life of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest survivors treated with extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation and their caregivers.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) are at risk of long-term neurological, cognitive, and psychological impairment, and this burden may extend to their caregivers. We evaluated long-term survival and multidimensional outcomes in survivors of refractory OHCA treated with extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) and in their caregivers.
METHODS: Adults discharged alive after ECPR for refractory OHCA at a tertiary centre (2013-2024) were included. Survivors underwent long-term assessment of functional status and cognition, and self-reported psychological well-being, sleep, fatigue, return to work, and quality of life (QoL). One caregiver per survivor was evaluated for psychological distress, QoL, fatigue, and perceived burden.
RESULTS: Among 406 ECPR-treated patients, 63 (16%) were discharged alive. At a median follow-up of 3.1 (IQR 0.6-6.9) years, 38/62 (61%) were alive, of whom 31 (82%) had favourable neurological outcome. Only 7 of all 406 treated patients (1.7%) were alive with poor neurological outcome. Five-year mortality was higher in patients discharged with poor versus favourable neurological status (86% vs. 13%, p < 0.001). Among the 17 survivors and 19 caregivers assessed, QoL was preserved and comparable between groups (EQ VAS 70 [60-80] vs 80 [75-90]). Most survivors and caregivers reported no limitations in mobility, self-care, or usual activities. Mild cognitive impairment was found in 6/16 survivors and poor sleep quality in 10/17. Anxiety symptoms were more frequent among caregivers than survivors (6/18 vs 1/17). No participant met criteria for symptomatic post-traumatic stress disorder. Seven of 15 previously employed survivors and all caregivers returned to work.
CONCLUSIONS: Long-term survival after ECPR was largely confined to patients with favourable neurological recovery. Despite preserved overall QoL, survivors frequently showed cognitive impairment and reported sleep disturbances. Anxiety symptoms were common among caregivers. These findings support structured long-term follow-up programmes for both survivors and their families.

title: Improving the safety and efficacy of whole blood resuscitation from hemorrhagic shock with a novel scavenger protein cocktail.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic shock is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in trauma and surgery. Although blood component therapy is the standard of care, whole blood (WB) transfusion is becoming more popular as it may provide volumetric, hemostatic, and O2-carrying capacity benefits. It is unclear if stored WB is more susceptible to hemolysis than blood components.
OBJECTIVES: This study evaluates a novel experimental scavenger protein cocktail (PC) designed to bind hemoglobin, heme, and iron, mitigating toxicity from acellular hemolytic byproducts and enhancing the safety profile of stored WB.
METHODS: Adult male Golden Syrian hamsters outfitted with a dorsal window chamber were subjected to hemorrhage, kept in hypovolemic shock for 30 min, and resuscitated via transfusion of stored WB with low, moderate, or severe hemolysis, or each stored WB group pretreated with PC.
RESULTS: Stored WB hemolysis showed a significant negative correlation with hematocrit, microvascular flow, and functional capillary density at 30 and 60 min post-transfusion. Stored WB hemolysis showed a significant positive correlation with markers of cardiovascular, renal, and hepatic injury, as well as blood lactate accumulation at 60 min. Pre-treating stored WB with PC mitigated functional capillary collapse and tissue injury in moderate- and high-hemolysis WB groups. The PC's oncotic effects produced hemodilution, and there was no significant recovery of hematocrit, pH, or lactate levels to baseline in the WB + PC groups.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that hemolysis in stored WB determines resuscitation outcomes, and optimizing PC additive dosing can improve the safety and efficacy of WB transfusion.

title: Sex differences in bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation and survival to hospital discharge for public out-of-hospital cardiac arrests in North Carolina and Singapore: a retrospective cohort study.
abstract:
AIM: Women are less likely to receive bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) in public. The study aims to assess if sex in patients with public out-of-hospital cardiac arrests (OHCAs), was associated with bystander CPR and survival to hospital discharge, in North Carolina and Singapore.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adult (≥18 years) OHCAs of the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (North Carolina, 2013-2022) and the Pan-Asian Resuscitation Outcomes Study (Singapore, 2010-2020). Using multivariable logistic regression, we examined the association of sex with bystander CPR and survival to hospital discharge adjusting for potential confounding variables (e.g. age, year of arrest).
RESULTS: We analyzed data from 6828 OHCAs in North Carolina and 3617 OHCAs in Singapore. Public bystander CPR rates were 48% for males and 44% for females in North Carolina [adjusted odd ratio (aOR) 0.87; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.77, 0.99], and 59% for males and 52% for females in Singapore [aOR 0.78; 95% CI (0.62, 0.98)]. The proportion surviving to hospital discharge in North Carolina were 24% for males and 26% for females [aOR 1.15; 95% CI (1.00, 1.33)], and 12% for males and 9% for females in Singapore [aOR 0.63; 95% CI (0.43, 0.93)].
CONCLUSION: Females were less likely to receive bystander CPR than males in public in both North Carolina and Singapore, irrespective of age. However, females were less likely to survive to hospital discharge compared to males in Singapore, whereas the opposite was seen in North Carolina.

title: Endotracheal intubation practices, success rates and adverse events in four Dutch emergency departments: a multicentre retrospective study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Endotracheal intubation in the emergency department (ED) is a high-risk intervention associated with significant complications. Contemporary European data on emergency airway management remain limited, and no published data are available from the Netherlands. This study aimed to describe endotracheal intubation practices, success rates, and adverse events in four Dutch EDs.
METHODS: We conducted a multicentre retrospective cohort study of patients undergoing endotracheal intubation in four teaching hospital EDs in the Netherlands between January 2019 and December 2023. Patients were identified using procedure registrations, diagnostic codes, billing information and disposition records. Trained abstractors collected standardized data on patient characteristics, indications, provider characteristics, intubation techniques, medications, first-pass success and adverse events.
RESULTS: A total of 1250 intubations were included. The most common indication was post-return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) after cardiac arrest (47%), followed by neurologic pathology (14%), cardiac arrest (12%), respiratory insufficiency (8%), intoxication (8%), and trauma (5%). Emergency medicine and intensive care physicians performed most intubations. Videolaryngoscopy was the primary technique in 89.5% of cases, and etomidate was the most frequently used induction agent (73.5%). The overall first-pass success rate was 93.8% and did not differ by provider specialty or level of training. Adverse events occurred in 181 patients (14.5%), with hypotension (6.5%) and desaturation (4.7%) being most common. Increasing age (OR 1.07 per year, 95% CI 1.04-1.10) and cardiac pathology as indication for intubation (OR 3.50, 95% CI 1.03-11.88) were associated with hypotension. A higher body mass index (OR 1.08 per point, 95% CI 1.03-1.13), younger age (OR 0.98 per year, 95% CI 0.96-1.00, p = 0.022) and multiple intubations attempts (OR 2.9, 95% CI 1.12-7.33) were associated with desaturation. Lower pre-intubation oxygen saturation was associated with peri-intubation cardiac arrest (OR 0.96 per point, 95% CI 0.92-0.99).
CONCLUSIONS: This study provides the first multicentre description of emergency airway management in Dutch EDs and demonstrates a distinctive emergency intubation population, characterised by a high proportion of post-ROSC intubations. Contemporary practice was characterised by widespread adoption of videolaryngoscopy, frequent use of etomidate, and high first-pass success rates. Peri-intubation hypotension and desaturation remained common and represent important targets for quality improvement.

title: Trauma undertriage at a University Hospital in North Norway: the need to look beyond mechanism of injury.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early multidisciplinary management through trauma team activation (TTA) improves outcomes for severely injured patients. Previous studies at the University Hospital of North Norway (UNN) Tromsø conducted in 2006 and 2013, using Injury Severity Score (ISS) ≥ 16 as reference, found high rates of undertriage at 32% and 28% respectively. The aim of this study was to assess the current undertriage at UNN Tromsø using both ISS ≥ 16 and the New Injury Severity Score (NISS) ≥ 16 as reference.
METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed trauma patients admitted to UNN Tromsø in 2018 and 2023. The study included all patients met with TTA as well as all severely injured patients that did not receive TTA during the period. Data were obtained from the local trauma registry and electronic medical records. Undertriage was defined as patients with ISS ≥ 16 and no TTA, and NISS ≥ 16 and no TTA.
RESULTS: A total of 527 trauma patients were included. Undertriage based on ISS was 15% overall for 2018 and 2023. When NISS ≥ 16 was applied, the undertriage increased to 18% (31/171). A total of 63% of undertriaged patients fulfilled one or more national TTA criteria but was not admitted with TTA. Low-energy falls were the predominant mechanism of injury (73%) among undertriaged patients. A total of 70% of undertriaged patients had single region injuries, and 40% had organ failure.
CONCLUSIONS: The undertriage rate at UNN Tromsø was 15% in 2018 and 2023, still exceeding the recommended level of < 5% according to American College of Surgeons-Committee on Trauma. Undertriage appears largely related to the system's non-compliance with trauma criteria, and injuries sustained in low-energy trauma mechanisms. Use of NISS identifies a larger group of potentially undertriaged patients, including more patients with organ failure who may benefit from TTA.

title: Early serum uric acid decline and 30-day survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
Bystander CPR Type and Outcomes After Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Compression-only cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CO-CPR) has been widely promoted to encourage bystander intervention in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but long-term trends in bystander CPR and the associations between CPR type and outcomes in pediatric OHCA remain unclear.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate temporal trends in bystander CPR type and the associations with clinical outcomes among children with OHCA in Japan.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This cohort study included patients aged 17 years or younger with known receipt of bystander CPR documented in the nationwide All-Japan Utstein Registry from January 1, 2005, to December 31, 2023. Data analysis was performed from November 24, 2025, to September 2, 2026, including additional analyses conducted during the revision process.
EXPOSURES: Bystander CPR was categorized as rescue-breathing CPR (RB-CPR), CO-CPR, or no bystander CPR.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was 30-day neurologically favorable survival rate; secondary outcomes were 30-day survival rate and prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Temporal trends were assessed with multinomial logistic regression, and associations between CPR type and outcomes were evaluated using modified Poisson regression with robust variance estimation, with CO-CPR serving as the reference.
RESULTS: Among 26 785 pediatric patients with OHCA (median [IQR] age, 2.0 [0-12] years; 16 254 males [60.7%]), 6543 (24.4%) received RB-CPR, 9112 (34.0%) received CO-CPR, and 11 130 (41.6%) received no bystander CPR. The adjusted probability of CO-CPR increased from 14.6% (95% CI, 13.1%-16.1%) in 2005 to 55.1% (95% CI, 52.5%-57.6%) in 2023, whereas RB-CPR declined from 41.7% (95% CI, 39.7%-43.7%) to 10.4% (95% CI, 8.7%-12.1%). The adjusted probability of receiving no bystander CPR plateaued at approximately 35.0% after 2013. Neurologically favorable 30-day survival rate occurred in 3.6% receiving no bystander CPR, 9.5% receiving CO-CPR, and 16.0% receiving RB-CPR. Compared with CO-CPR, RB-CPR was associated with a higher 30-day neurologically favorable survival rate (adjusted risk ratio [ARR], 1.71; 95% CI, 1.57-1.86), 30-day survival rate (ARR, 1.51; 95% CI, 1.42-1.61), and prehospital ROSC (ARR, 1.62; 95% CI, 1.51-1.75), whereas receipt of no bystander CPR was associated with lower probabilities of these outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this cohort study of children with OHCA, increasing CO-CPR use coincided with declining RB-CPR but not with further reductions in untreated arrests after 2013. No bystander CPR was associated with worse outcomes compared with CO-CPR and RB-CPR. RB-CPR had more favorable outcomes than CO-CPR, supporting the continued importance of rescue breathing in pediatric resuscitation.

title: Timing of Antenatal Care, Stillbirth, and Infant Mortality in Migrant Mothers in Australia.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Timely antenatal care (ANC) reduces pregnancy risks, yet the association between delayed ANC and stillbirth or infant mortality among migrant mothers in Australia has not previously been investigated.
OBJECTIVE: To examine whether delayed ANC is associated with higher stillbirth and infant mortality among Australia-born compared with migrant mothers.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This retrospective cohort study assessed births to non-Indigenous mothers in New South Wales from January 1, 2002, to December 31, 2020, followed up to infant age of 1 year. Mothers were categorized as Australia-born, migrant from English-speaking country (ESM), or migrant from non-English-speaking country (non-ESM). Data were analyzed between August 2025 and June 2026.
EXPOSURES: Timing of first ANC, defined as 12 weeks or earlier, 13 to 19 weeks, 20 weeks or later, or no ANC.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The main outcome was stillbirth (at ≥20 weeks) and infant mortality (at prehospital discharge, posthospital discharge, or 1 year). Adjusted relative risks (ARRs) were estimated using Poisson regression models, stratified by migration group.
RESULTS: This study included 1 720 033 births (median [IQR] maternal age, 31.2 [27.4-34.8] years; 884 235 male infants [51.4%]), including 1 132 193 (65.8%) to Australia-born, 116 026 (6.7%) to ESM, and 471 814 (27.4%) to non-ESM mothers. Late ANC (>12 weeks) was more common in non-ESM mothers (190 338 [40.3%]) than Australia-born (334 790 [29.6%]) or ESM (41 029 [35.4%]) mothers. In cross-group comparisons, non-ESM mother status was associated with higher risk of adverse outcomes regardless of ANC timing. Compared with Australia-born mothers with early ANC (≤12 weeks), a higher risk of stillbirth (ARR, 1.25; 95% CI, 1.18-1.33) and 1-year (ARR, 1.32; 95% CI, 1.22-1.44), predischarge (ARR, 1.39; 95% CI, 1.25-1.54), and postdischarge (ARR, 1.19; 95% CI, 1.03-1.37) infant mortality was observed in non-ESM mothers accessing ANC by 12 weeks. Similar risk patterns were observed in non-ESM mothers with late ANC. In within-group comparisons, among Australia-born mothers, each category of delayed ANC was associated with higher risk. No ANC was associated with the highest risks across all maternal groups for stillbirth and 1-year infant mortality. For non-ESM mothers, late ANC (≥20 weeks) was associated with a lower risk of predischarge mortality (ARR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.61-0.92) but a higher risk of postdischarge mortality (ARR, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.02-1.65).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this cohort study of 1.72 million births, higher risks of stillbirths and infant mortalities were observed in non-ESM mothers regardless of ANC timing, warranting further investigation.

title: Sudden Deaths From Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage and Proximity to Neurosurgical Tertiary Care.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: A substantial proportion of deaths due to aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) occur without admission to neurosurgical units. Whether this proportion varies by geographic region is unclear.
OBJECTIVE: To determine the proportion of SAH deaths without neurosurgical unit admission across hospital districts in 2 high-income countries.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This retrospective, population-based cohort study used 2 externally validated nationwide administrative data collections in all 41 hospital districts and 10 neurosurgical units in Finland and New Zealand from January 1, 2001, to December 31, 2017. Participants included all hospitalized and fatal nonhospitalized cases with SAH. Data were analyzed from July 1, 2024, to September 7, 2026.
EXPOSURES: Hospital district of residence and its distance to the designated neurosurgical referral center, grouped into 4 zones.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was the death-based proportion of all 30-day deaths after SAH that occurred without neurosurgical unit admission (prehospital deaths plus deaths within 30 days after admission to a nonneurosurgical unit divided by all 30-day deaths from SAH). This proportion was estimated across 41 hospital districts and demographic groups, with age- and sex-adjusted risk ratios (RRs) and 95% CIs.
RESULTS: A total of 12 912 patients with SAH (7856 in Finland and 5056 in New Zealand; median age, 58 [IQR, 49-69] years; 7924 [61.4%] women) were included. Of all 5418 SAH deaths, 3819 (70.5%) occurred without neurosurgical unit admission: 2203 of 3114 (70.7%) in Finland (interdistrict range, 403 of 644 [62.6%] to 5 of 5 [100%]) and 1616 of 2304 (70.1%) in New Zealand (interdistrict range, 111 of 190 [58.4%] to 22 of 23 [95.7%]). Compared with districts containing a neurosurgical unit (1723 of 2602 [66.2%]), the death-based proportions were higher in close-distance (1-130 km; 796 of 1129 [70.5%]; RR, 1.07 [95% CI, 1.02-1.12]), middle-distance (131-157 km; 469 of 599 [78.3%]; RR, 1.18 [95% CI, 1.12-1.24]), and far-distance (158-371 km; 831 of 1088 [76.4%]; RR, 1.15 [95% CI, 1.10-1.20]) zones. This proportion increased by 6.7% (95% CI, 4.9%-8.5%) for each additional 100 km to a neurosurgical unit. The proportions decreased in both countries over time.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this cohort study of 12 912 patients with SAH, most deaths occurred without neurosurgical unit admission, and this proportion increased with distance to the neurosurgical referral center. Prevention and early management outside tertiary care may therefore warrant priority in reducing SAH mortality.

title: Mass Cytometry revealed endothelial-Ly6C+IMs crosstalk to exacerbate heatstroke induced acute lung injury.
abstract: Acute lung injury (ALI) is a common complication of heatstroke (HS). Within the inflamed lung microenvironment, endothelial cells (ECs) are known to orchestrate the phenotypic and functional reprogramming of immune cells, particularly macrophages. However, the exact mechanism by which ECs reshape macrophage phenotypes in HS-ALI remains poorly understood. In this study, we integrated mass cytometry (CyTOF), flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, western blotting, and immunofluorescence to comprehensively map the pulmonary immune landscape and elucidate endothelial-macrophage crosstalk in HS-ALI. Our results reveal dynamic changes of leukocyte components during HS, involving CD4+T, CD8+T, and γδT lymphocytes, DCs, NK cells, alveolar macrophages (AMs), interstitial macrophages (IMs), and monocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells (M-MDSCs). Functionally, we identified that pro-inflammatory (M1-like) Ly6C+ IMs differentiate from M-MDSCs. Furthermore, HS triggered robust engagement between pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells (PMVECs) and IMs, a process potentially mediated by endothelial CXCL2 signaling. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that ECs serve as critical regulators of the differentiation and function of M-MDSC-derived Ly6C+ IMs, offering a promising therapeutic target for HS-ALI.

title: CD47-dependent myeloid reprogramming drives IL-10-mediated T-cell suppression in heatstroke.
abstract: Heatstroke can trigger immune dysregulation, yet the mechanisms driving progression to critical illness remain poorly understood. Here, we integrate bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing with functional studies to characterize heatstroke-associated immunosuppression. Transcriptomic profiling of peripheral blood mononuclear cells from heatstroke patients revealed a transition from enhanced innate immune responses in mild heatstroke to marked adaptive immune suppression in critical disease. Disease progression was associated with increased S100A8/A12 and IL-10 expression and reduced T-cell- and HLA-associated gene expression. Myeloid-derived suppressor cell (MDSC) signatures correlated inversely with CD8⁺ T-cell abundance and cytotoxicity and positively with IL-10 levels and disease severity. Single-cell analyses revealed depletion of T and NK cells, myeloid expansion, MDSC accumulation, and reduced T-cell clonality. Pseudotime and RNA velocity analyses further indicated that heatstroke redirects myeloid differentiation towards an immunosuppressive MDSC state. In mice, CD47 blockade restrained MDSC expansion and IL-10 production, restored T-cell function, reduced organ injury, and improved survival. These findings identify myeloid reprogramming and MDSC-mediated T-cell suppression as mechanisms of heatstroke-associated immune dysfunction and support CD47 blockade as a potential therapeutic strategy.
