title: Flexible Ultralow-Power IGZO Multimodal Synaptic Transistors for Thermally Robust Neuromorphic Vision and Wearable Heatstroke Monitoring.
abstract: Multimodal synaptic devices are increasingly required to enable more reliable and informed decision-making in next-generation neuromorphic systems. A wafer-scale, energy-efficient flexible optoelectronic synaptic transistor based on an a-IGZO channel and ALD-deposited HfO2 gate dielectric is demonstrated. The device is fabricated on a rigid silicon substrate and subsequently transformed into a flexible form, maintaining stable electrical characteristics under repeated bending (radius ∼3 cm). The device enables multimodal sensing by responding to optical stimulus and a wide temperature range (10-75°C), capturing signals such as body temperature, ambient conditions, and sunlight. Under optical stimulation, the transistor emulates key synaptic functions, including EPSC, PPF, and the transition from STM to LTM, as well as learning-forgetting-relearning behavior. Reliable synaptic responses are achieved at a low drain voltage of 0.01 V, with an energy consumption of 1.6 fJ per synaptic event. The behavior is governed by defect-mediated carrier trapping and detrapping in IGZO. System-level applications include heatstroke risk classification (99.6% accuracy, within the physiological temperature range 37°C-42°C) and neuromorphic vision sensing enabled by persistent photoconductivity. These multimodal capabilities enable both heatstroke monitoring and thermally robust vision processing within a unified platform. The results present a scalable platform for low-power neuromorphic and wearable healthcare applications.

title: The effects of common emergency call system applications in pre-hospital emergency medical services from a lean management perspective: The case of Ordu province, Turkiye.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the impact of a centralized Common Emergency Call Center (CECC) system on prehospital emergency medical services (EMS) efficiency through the lens of Lean Management principles.
METHODOLOGY: This retrospective, longitudinal study analyzed secondary data from Ordu province, Turkey, comparing a 36 months pre-CECC period (2018-2020) with a 48 months post-CECC period (2021-2024). The dataset comprised 2,346,774 calls and 721,897 cases. Key performance indicators, selected as proxies for lean waste (communication, time, transport), were compared using independent samples t-tests.
RESULTS: Following CECC implementation, significant improvements were observed (p<0.001). The call-per-incident ratio, a proxy for communication waste, decreased by 49.0% (from 4.63 to 2.36). Time-based waste was reduced, with respond time of ambulance teams falling by 36.9% and ambulance mobilization time by 23.7%. Transportation waste, measured by distance per incident, decreased by 15.1%. On-time arrival rates improved significantly in both urban (93.9% to 98.4%) and rural (82.2% to 89.2%) areas. These gains were achieved without a statistically significant increase in the patient load coefficient.
CONCLUSION: The centralized CECC system, acting as a structural lean intervention, significantly reduced operational waste and improved efficiency in prehospital EMS. This centralized CECC model offers a scalable blueprint for health systems seeking to enhance emergency care delivery.

title: Debriefing in prehospital simulation-based education: a scoping review of ambulance nurse and paramedic literature.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Simulation is fundamental to the education of paramedics and ambulance nurses, with debriefing widely recognised as the educational component through which much of the learning is consolidated. However, how debriefing is implemented and reported within prehospital simulation for practising clinicians remains poorly understood. This scoping review mapped and critically examined debriefing approaches used in simulation involving paramedics, ambulance nurses, flight paramedics, and flight nurses.
METHODS: Using Arksey and O'Malley's (2005) scoping review framework and the PRISMA-ScR reporting guideline, MEDLINE, EMCARE, CINAHL Plus, SCOPUS, and Google Scholar were searched for studies published in English or Arabic between 2005 and 2025. Following editorial review, all included studies were re-examined against the predefined eligibility criteria, and studies involving student-only populations were excluded. Findings were charted and synthesised thematically.
RESULTS: From 974 identified records, 18 studies met the final inclusion criteria. Most studies originated from the United States, employed quantitative designs, and were published between 2012 and 2025. Two themes were identified: guided debriefing (n = 15) and tool- and technology-assisted debriefing (n = 3). Across the included literature, debriefing was associated with improvements in technical performance, communication, teamwork, clinical reasoning, and reflective practice. However, reporting of debriefing interventions remained inconsistent, with considerable variation in facilitation, structure, outcome measures, and theoretical underpinning. Many studies relied on self-reported educational outcomes, making it difficult to distinguish the specific contribution of debriefing from the broader effects of simulation-based education.
CONCLUSION: Debriefing remains a central component of prehospital simulation-based education for practising clinicians, yet its design and reporting vary considerably across the literature. Guided debriefing was the predominant approach, while evidence supporting technology-assisted debriefing was comparatively limited. Future research should adopt clearer descriptions of debriefing interventions, strengthen theoretical and pedagogical foundations, and incorporate objective measures of learner performance to better understand how different debriefing approaches influence clinical practice.

title: Research on a prediction model for outcomes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation in community out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients based on the Utstein model.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To construct an automated machine learning (AutoML)-based prediction model for cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) outcomes in community out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients using the Utstein model, systematically identify key predictive factors, and provide a basis for clinical risk stratification and individualized intervention.
METHODS: A single-center retrospective study design was employed, including all adult non-traumatic OHCA patients managed by the Emergency Department of The First People's Hospital of Lin'an District, Hangzhou, from March 2019 to March 2024. All OHCA patients were analyzed to identify key factors associated with achieving return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). In the second stage, a sub-cohort of patients who successfully achieved ROSC was selected to further investigate predictors influencing their 30-day survival status, ultimately developing the final prognostic prediction model. The Improved Fast Tree-seed Algorithm (IFATA) was utilized within the AutoML framework to optimize model hyperparameters. Feature importance was validated through dual-dimensional LASSO regression and SHAP interpretability models. An interactive web-based clinical decision support tool was developed for risk assessment and clinical communication.
RESULTS: Among 370 enrolled patients, 256 (69.19%) died after resuscitation, while 114 (30.81%) achieved ROSC. The AutoML model demonstrated comprehensive optimal performance, with a ROC-AUC of 0.9891 and PR-AUC of 0.9490. Key features selected by AutoML were: on-site defibrillation, cumulative epinephrine dosage, time from cardiac arrest (CA) to CPR initiation, time from CA to endotracheal intubation, PCO2, and time from CA to intravenous access establishment. When evaluated on the test set, AutoML exhibited the strongest robustness, achieving a ROC-AUC of 0.9815 and PR-AUC of 0.9515. Its predictive calibration significantly outperformed other models, with the lowest Brier score (0.127). SHAP analysis ranked feature importance as follows: on-site defibrillation > cumulative epinephrine dosage > time from CA to CPR initiation > time from CA to endotracheal intubation > PCO2 > time from CA to intravenous access establishment.
CONCLUSION: By integrating multidimensional clinical data with interpretable machine learning techniques, this study confirms the core role of the Utstein model in predicting CPR outcomes for OHCA patients. It achieves real-time translation of risk assessment into intervention decisions, providing innovative tools and methodologies for precise OHCA resuscitation.

title: Epidemiology, outcomes, and associated factors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in Zhejiang, China: a province-wide registry study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains a major public health challenge with poor survival worldwide. Although previous studies have described OHCA epidemiology and outcomes in China, province-wide data comprehensively characterizing patient and arrest characteristics, clinical outcomes, and factors associated with survival and neurological recovery remain limited.
OBJECTIVES: To characterize the epidemiology and outcomes of OHCA and identify factors associated with 30-day survival and favorable neurological outcome in Zhejiang, China.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective analysis of prospectively collected data from the Zhejiang Emergency Registry (ZER), a mandatory province-wide emergency medical services (EMS) registry based on Utstein-style standardized reporting in Zhejiang, China. Adult EMS-treated OHCA cases of medical etiology between January 2024 and December 2025 were included. Patient characteristics, arrest circumstances, community response, dispatcher-related factors, EMS characteristics, prehospital interventions, and clinical outcomes were described. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with 30-day survival and favorable neurological outcome.
RESULTS: Among 17,646 EMS-treated OHCA patients, 531 (3.0%) survived to 30 days and 345 (2.0%) achieved favorable neurological outcome. Bystander CPR was performed in 47.7% of cases, while dispatcher recognition of OHCA, dispatcher-assisted CPR, and bystander automated external defibrillator (AED) use occurred in 25.1%, 20.0%, and 1.8% of cases, respectively. Home arrests accounted for 64.3% of cases and had a 30-day survival rate of 2.2%. Both 30-day survival and favorable neurological outcome progressively declined with increasing EMS response time. In multivariable analysis, shockable rhythm showed the strongest association with both 30-day survival and favorable neurological outcome. Younger age, witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, bystander AED use, dispatcher recognition, dispatcher-assisted CPR, and shorter EMS response time were independently associated with improved 30-day survival.
CONCLUSION: In this province-wide registry study, 30-day survival and favorable neurological outcomes after OHCA remained low in Zhejiang, China. Low rates of dispatcher recognition, dispatcher-assisted CPR, and bystander AED use were observed, and outcomes declined progressively with increasing EMS response time. Several factors were independently associated with 30-day survival and favorable neurological outcome. These findings provide population-level evidence to inform future quality-improvement strategies for OHCA care.

title: Integrating clinical research into emergency medical services: lessons from the PreMeFen trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Clinical research in the pre-hospital setting is essential to advance evidence-based care. However, integrating research into emergency medical services (EMS) is challenging, as trial protocols must coexist with delivery of time-critical patient care. The PreMeFen randomised controlled trial, undertaken in a regional EMS system in Norway, provided an opportunity to examine operational challenges related to trial conduct and implementation through the experiences of ambulance personnel and linked trial process data.
METHODS: This was a cross-sectional survey addressing training, motivation, communication, and experiences related to trial conduct in the pre-hospital setting. Ambulance personnel who had at least one patient in the PreMeFen trial were invited to participate. Descriptive statistics summarised survey responses. Additional data included protocol adherence, deviations, and communication logs collected during the 18-month PreMeFen trial period.
RESULTS: Of 70 invited ambulance personnel, 67 (96%) responded. Most felt well prepared following mandatory training, and 65 (97%) found training beneficial. Initial motivation to participate was high (median 8, inter quartile range (IQR) 8-10), but declined over time (median 7, IQR 5-8). Among 338 patient inclusions, 94 (28%) protocol deviations were recorded, most occurring early in the trial period, where missing measurements were the most common cause. Communication from the central study team was extensive. Although 60 (90%) felt well informed, 34 (51%) found the information excessive. Despite these challenges, 60 (90%) expressed willingness to participate in future research.
CONCLUSION: Integrating clinical research into EMS is feasible but can be operationally demanding. Adequate training, ongoing support, and balanced communication appear to be important for maintaining motivation and protocol adherence among ambulance personnel involved in clinical studies.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: The randomised controlled trial component of this study was registered in ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05137184) and EudraCT (2021-000549-42).

title: Face-Blind but Cyborg-Sighted: Immunological Barriers to the Patient-Paramedic Articulation.
abstract: Immunity is the body's concept of recognizing where one's self ends and non-self begins. The paramedic (oneself)/patient (non-self) barrier has long been institutionalized; healthcare workers are trained to disarticulate from the patient to reduce physical and infectious harm to self. Harm may include psychological trauma and post-traumatic stress disorder, especially routinely witnessing people in distress. Using magical realism in experimental autoethnographic reflection, the author applies established conceptualizations of "articulation" to his experiences as a prosopagnosiac, transgender person, and paramedic while exploring how applying the Science and Technology Studies concept of "articulation" to healthcare can reduce trauma in care settings.
